questions.prompt: The hikers were confused by the directions. They checked the map. Which sentence correctly combines the ideas with a participial phrase that describes the hikers' state?
choices: Confused by the directions, the hikers checked the map.
Checking the map, the hikers were confused by the directions.
The directions, confused by the hikers, were difficult to understand.
Confused by the map, the hikers checked the directions.
questions.explanation: The opening participial phrase describes the hikers' state and correctly modifies the subject of the main clause.
questions.topic: Activity 3 of 9: Combine Two Sentences - Advanced Grammar Review

questions.prompt: The parcel was delayed. The manager wanted to know when. Which sentence correctly combines the ideas with a what-clause?
choices: What the manager wanted to know was when the parcel was delayed.
What the manager wanted to know were when the parcel was delayed.
What the manager wanted to know was the time the parcel was delayed when.
What the manager wanted to know was because the parcel was delayed.
questions.explanation: The what-clause serves as the subject, and the was clause identifies the information the manager wanted.
questions.topic: Combine Two Sentences - Advanced Grammar Review

questions.prompt: The rain started. We moved the game indoors. Which sentence uses so to express the cause-and-effect relationship?
choices: The rain started, so we moved the game indoors.
The rain started because we moved the game indoors.
The rain started, although we moved the game indoors.
The rain started, and we moved the game indoors.
questions.explanation: The coordinating conjunction so follows a comma to show that the rain caused the game to be moved indoors.
questions.topic: Combine Two Sentences - Advanced Grammar Review

questions.prompt: Nora is a volunteer coach. She runs Saturday drills. Which sentence correctly combines the ideas with an appositive?
choices: Nora, a volunteer coach, runs Saturday drills.
Nora, who is a volunteer coach runs Saturday drills.
Nora a volunteer coach runs Saturday drills.
Nora, a volunteer coach; she runs Saturday drills.
questions.explanation: The appositive a volunteer coach identifies Nora and is correctly enclosed by commas on both sides.
questions.topic: Activity 3 of 9 (quiz/game): Combine Two Sentences - Advanced Grammar Review

questions.prompt: The final bell rang. The class ended early. Which sentence combines the ideas with an absolute phrase?
choices: The final bell having rung the class ended early.
The final bell had rung, the class ended early.
The final bell having rung, it ended the class early.
The final bell having rung, the class ended early.
questions.explanation: The noun phrase the final bell having rung is an absolute phrase set off by a comma before the main clause.
questions.topic: Combine Two Sentences - Advanced Grammar Review

questions.prompt: The northern trail was muddy. The southern trail was dry. Which sentence combines the ideas with a subordinating conjunction that expresses contrast?
choices: The northern trail was muddy, because the southern trail was dry.
The northern trail was muddy, since the southern trail was dry.
The northern trail was muddy, whereas the southern trail was dry.
The northern trail was muddy, if the southern trail was dry.
questions.explanation: Whereas signals a direct contrast between the muddy northern trail and the dry southern trail.
questions.topic: Combine Two Sentences - Advanced Grammar Review

questions.prompt: The rehearsal ended early. The actors left the stage. Which sentence correctly combines the two independent clauses with a coordinating conjunction?
choices: The rehearsal ended early, and the actors left the stage.
The rehearsal ended early and, the actors left the stage.
The rehearsal ended early; and the actors left the stage.
The rehearsal ended early, the and actors left the stage.
questions.explanation: A comma before and separates two independent clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction.
questions.topic: Combine Two Sentences - Advanced Grammar Review

questions.prompt: The evidence was clear. Everyone understood it. Which sentence correctly combines the ideas with the correlative conjunction so...that?
choices: The evidence was so clear that everyone understood it.
The evidence was such clear that everyone understood it.
The evidence was so clearly that everyone understood it.
The evidence was so clear everyone understood it.
questions.explanation: The correlative pair so...that links the degree of the evidence's clarity with the result that everyone understood it.
questions.topic: Activity 3 of 9 (quiz/game): Combine Two Sentences - Advanced Grammar Review

questions.prompt: The museum will open early. The train arrives by ten. Which sentence combines the ideas using provided that to express a condition?
choices: If the train arrives by ten, the museum will open early.
The museum will open early provided that the train arrives by ten.
The museum will open early because the train arrives by ten.
The museum will open early when the train arrives by ten.
questions.explanation: Provided that introduces the condition under which the museum will open early.
questions.topic: Activity 3 of 9 (quiz/game): Combine Two Sentences - Advanced Grammar Review

questions.prompt: Maya designed the poster. It hangs above the bulletin board. Which sentence combines the two ideas using a relative clause?
choices: The poster that Maya designed hangs above the bulletin board.
The poster hangs above the bulletin board that Maya designed.
The poster that Maya designed it hangs above the bulletin board.
The poster that designed by Maya hangs above the bulletin board.
questions.explanation: The relative clause that Maya designed modifies poster and leaves the main clause with the verb hangs.
questions.skill: Combining sentences with a relative clause
questions.topic: Combine Two Sentences - Advanced Grammar Review

questions.prompt: The greenhouse is beside the garden. Seedlings grow there under filtered light. Which sentence correctly combines the ideas with a nonrestrictive relative clause?
choices: The greenhouse, which is beside the garden, is where seedlings grow under filtered light.
The greenhouse is beside the garden, where seedlings grow under filtered light.
The seedlings grow under filtered light, which is the greenhouse beside the garden.
Under the filtered light in the greenhouse, the seedlings grow beside the garden.
questions.explanation: The nonrestrictive clause which is beside the garden adds information about the greenhouse without restricting the meaning of the noun.
questions.topic: Activity 3 of 9: Combine Two Sentences - Advanced Grammar Review

questions.prompt: The evidence was strong. The team changed its plan. Which sentence uses however to show contrast and punctuates it correctly?
choices: The evidence was strong; however, the team changed its plan.
The evidence was strong, however, the team changed its plan.
The evidence was strong however, the team changed its plan.
The evidence was strong, however the team changed its plan.
questions.explanation: The semicolon separates the independent clauses, and the comma after the conjunctive adverb however correctly marks the contrast.
questions.topic: Combine Two Sentences - Advanced Grammar Review

questions.prompt: You can enter with a student ID. You can enter with a guest pass. Which sentence correctly combines the two options with the correlative conjunction either...or?
choices: You can enter with either a student ID or a guest pass.
You can enter with either a student ID and a guest pass.
You can enter with either a student ID nor a guest pass.
You can enter with either a student ID or a guest passes.
questions.explanation: The paired conjunctions either and or correctly offer two alternatives, and the noun phrases a student ID and a guest pass agree in form.
questions.topic: Combine Two Sentences - Advanced Grammar Review

questions.prompt: Which explanation best identifies why the introductory clause in After the movie ended, we discussed the ending is followed by a comma?
choices: The subordinating conjunction after is always followed by a comma.
The main clause must be separated from its subject because the clause is lengthy.
The introductory dependent clause is separated from the main clause by a comma.
The word ending modifies the movie and needs a comma to mark that relationship.
questions.explanation: A comma conventionally separates an introductory dependent clause from the main clause that follows it.
questions.topic: Combine Two Sentences - Advanced Grammar Review

questions.prompt: The technician spoke to the customer. The customer's printer had a paper jam. Which sentence combines the ideas using a possessive relative clause?
choices: The technician spoke to the customer, which printer had a paper jam.
The technician spoke to the customer, whose printer had a paper jam.
The technician spoke to the customer, who printer had a paper jam.
The technician spoke to the customer, whom printer had a paper jam.
questions.explanation: The possessive relative pronoun whose correctly links the customer to the clause describing the customer's printer.
questions.topic: Combine Two Sentences - Advanced Grammar Review

questions.prompt: The engineer inspected the bridge. It had several hairline cracks. Which sentence correctly combines the ideas using a relative clause?
choices: The engineer inspected the bridge, which had several hairline cracks.
The engineer inspected the bridge, who had several hairline cracks.
The engineer inspected the bridge, where had several hairline cracks.
The engineer inspected the bridge, whose had several hairline cracks.
questions.explanation: The relative pronoun which correctly refers to the bridge and incorporates the information about its cracks.
questions.skill: Combining ideas with a relative clause
questions.topic: Combine Two Sentences - Advanced Grammar Review

questions.prompt: The assistant drafted a checklist. He wanted the new volunteers to be prepared. Which sentence correctly combines the ideas with so that?
choices: The assistant drafted a checklist so that the new volunteers would prepare.
The assistant drafted a checklist so that the new volunteers would be prepared.
The assistant drafted a checklist so that the new volunteers being prepared.
The assistant drafted a checklist so that prepare the new volunteers.
questions.explanation: The so that clause expresses the intended result of drafting the checklist, while would be prepared preserves the volunteers as the passive subject.
questions.skill: Combining an action and its purpose with so that
questions.topic: Combine Two Sentences - Advanced Grammar Review

questions.prompt: The lights went out. The emergency signs appeared immediately. Which sentence presents the signs as appearing right after the lights failed?
choices: As soon as the lights went out, the emergency signs appeared.
Until the lights went out, the emergency signs appeared.
Although the lights went out, the emergency signs appeared.
Unless the lights went out, the emergency signs appeared.
questions.explanation: As soon as introduces a subordinate clause that shows the signs appeared immediately after the lights failed.
questions.skill: Combining sentences with a time conjunction
questions.topic: Combine Two Sentences - Advanced Grammar Review

questions.prompt: The score was excellent. One judge noted a missing citation. Which sentence correctly combines the ideas with the coordinating conjunction however and appropriate punctuation?
choices: The score was excellent; however, one judge noted a missing citation.
The score was excellent, however, one judge noted a missing citation.
The score was excellent: however, one judge noted a missing citation.
The score was excellent however, one judge noted a missing citation.
questions.explanation: A semicolon joins the independent clauses, and however is followed by a comma when it begins the second clause.
questions.topic: Combine Two Sentences - Advanced Grammar Review

questions.prompt: Which explanation correctly analyzes this complete sentence: When the bus was full, the driver waited for more passengers?
choices: The clause beginning with when is a subordinate clause with a subject and verb, while the main clause also has a subject and verb.
The clause beginning with when is a coordinating conjunction that joins two independent clauses.
The clause beginning with when has no verb, while the main clause supplies the missing subject.
The word when makes both clauses independent, so the sentence needs no main clause.
questions.explanation: The when clause is a complete subordinate clause, and the driver waited for more passengers is the complete main clause.
questions.skill: Explaining the structure of a combined sentence
questions.topic: Combine Two Sentences - Advanced Grammar Review

questions.prompt: The robot sorted the boxes. It also checked each label. Which sentence correctly uses the correlative conjunction not only...but also?
choices: The robot not only sorted the boxes but also checked each label.
The robot either sorted the boxes but also checked each label.
The robot not only sorted the boxes however also checked each label.
The robot neither sorted the boxes but also checked each label.
questions.explanation: Not only and but also form a matched pair that joins two coordinated actions in one sentence.
questions.topic: Combine Two Sentences - Advanced Grammar Review

questions.prompt: The workshop requires three supplies. The supplies are a pen, a notebook, and a pair of scissors. Which sentence correctly introduces the list with a colon?
choices: The workshop requires three supplies: a pen, a notebook, and a pair of scissors.
The workshop requires three supplies, a pen, a notebook, and a pair of scissors.
The workshop requires three supplies; a pen, a notebook, and a pair of scissors.
The workshop requires three supplies because a pen, a notebook, and a pair of scissors.
questions.explanation: The colon appropriately introduces the complete list of supplies after the introductory statement.
questions.skill: Using a colon to introduce a list
questions.topic: Combine Two Sentences - Advanced Grammar Review

questions.prompt: Keep the emergency exit clear. The last student passes through it. Which sentence combines the directions and the event correctly with until?
choices: Keep the emergency exit clear until the last student passes through it.
Keep the emergency exit clear until the last student passing through it.
Keep the emergency exit clear while the last student will pass through it.
Keep the emergency exit clear unless the last student passes through it.
questions.explanation: The clause until the last student passes through it correctly limits how long the emergency exit must remain clear.
questions.topic: Combine Two Sentences - Advanced Grammar Review

questions.prompt: A retired engineer designed the pedestrian bridge. The bridge crosses the river. Which sentence correctly combines the ideas with a relative clause?
choices: A retired engineer who designed the pedestrian bridge crosses the river.
The pedestrian bridge that the retired engineer designed crosses the river.
The retired engineer designed the pedestrian bridge that it crosses the river.
The pedestrian bridge crosses the river that the retired engineer designed.
questions.explanation: The relative clause that the retired engineer designed identifies which pedestrian bridge crosses the river.
questions.skill: Combining sentences with a relative clause
questions.topic: Combine Two Sentences - Advanced Grammar Review

questions.prompt: Ms. Delgado is the new librarian. She has reorganized the reading room. Which sentence combines the two ideas using an appositive?
choices: Ms. Delgado, the new librarian, has reorganized the reading room.
Ms. Delgado, who is the new librarian, has reorganized the reading room.
Ms. Delgado the new librarian has reorganized the reading room.
Ms. Delgado, the new librarian has reorganized the reading room.
questions.explanation: The appositive the new librarian renames Ms. Delgado and is set off by a pair of commas.
questions.topic: Combine Two Sentences - Advanced Grammar Review

questions.prompt: The road was closed for repairs. We took a different route. Which sentence makes the road closure the reason for taking another route?
choices: Although the road was closed for repairs, we took a different route.
Since the road was closed for repairs, we took a different route.
Unless the road was closed for repairs, we took a different route.
While the road was closed for repairs, we took a different route.
questions.explanation: Since introduces a subordinate clause that gives the reason for taking a different route.
questions.skill: Combining sentences to express a reason
questions.topic: Combine Two Sentences - Advanced Grammar Review

questions.prompt: The editor cut the final paragraph. She wanted the article to fit on one page. Which sentence combines the ideas by beginning with an infinitive phrase?
choices: To make the article fit on one page, the editor cut the final paragraph.
For making the article fit on one page, the editor cut the final paragraph.
By make the article fit on one page, the editor cut the final paragraph.
The editor cut the final paragraph, to make the article fit on one page.
questions.explanation: To make the article fit on one page is an infinitive phrase that expresses the editor's purpose.
questions.topic: Combine Two Sentences - Advanced Grammar Review

questions.prompt: The music played. At the same time, the dancers rehearsed their steps. Which version preserves the simultaneous timing between the music and the rehearsal?
choices: Because the music played, the dancers rehearsed their steps.
Unless the music played, the dancers rehearsed their steps.
Although the music played, the dancers rehearsed their steps.
While the music played, the dancers rehearsed their steps.
questions.explanation: While introduces a subordinate clause that shows the dancers rehearsed while the music was playing.
questions.skill: Combining sentences with a temporal subordinate clause
questions.topic: Combine Two Sentences - Advanced Grammar Review

questions.prompt: Dr. Patel is a marine biologist. She presented her latest research yesterday. Which sentence correctly combines the ideas using an appositive?
choices: Dr. Patel, a marine biologist presented her latest research yesterday.
Dr. Patel, a marine biologist, presented her latest research yesterday.
Dr. Patel a marine biologist, presented her latest research yesterday.
Dr. Patel, marine biologist, presented her latest research yesterday.
questions.explanation: The appositive a marine biologist identifies Dr. Patel and is correctly enclosed by commas.
questions.topic: Combine Two Sentences - Advanced Grammar Review

questions.prompt: The bell rang. Everyone left the gym. Which explanation best identifies why the semicolon correctly joins these two independent clauses?
choices: The two independent clauses are closely related, so a semicolon joins them without creating a comma splice.
The second clause is dependent on the first, so a semicolon completes the shared subject and verb.
The two clauses have different subjects, so a semicolon can replace the missing verb in the second clause.
The first clause contains a prepositional phrase, so a semicolon separates it from the main clause.
questions.explanation: The semicolon marks the boundary between two closely related independent clauses without incorrectly joining them with only a comma.
questions.topic: Combine Two Sentences - Advanced Grammar Review

questions.prompt: Suppose the school extends the deadline. Students will have more time to revise. Which sentence combines the ideas as an unreal condition using the second conditional?
choices: If the school extends the deadline, students will have more time to revise.
If the school extended the deadline, students would have more time to revise.
If the school would extend the deadline, students will have more time to revise.
If the school had extended the deadline, students would have had more time to revise.
questions.explanation: The second conditional uses a past-tense if-clause and would followed by a base verb to frame the deadline extension as hypothetical.
questions.skill: Combining sentences with the second conditional
questions.topic: Combine Two Sentences - Advanced Grammar Review

questions.prompt: The alarm sounded. The students left because of the alarm. Which sentence combines the ideas with a that-clause introduced by the reason?
choices: The reason the alarm sounded was that the students left the building.
The reason the students left the building was because the alarm sounded.
The reason the students left the building was that the alarm sounded.
The reason of the students left the building was that the alarm sounded.
questions.explanation: The construction the reason the students left the building was that the alarm sounded presents the alarm as the reason for the students' departure.
questions.topic: Combine Two Sentences - Advanced Grammar Review

questions.prompt: The curator unlocked the gallery at noon. The visitors entered at 12:05. Which sentence correctly combines the ideas with the subordinating conjunction after?
choices: After the curator unlocked the gallery at noon, the visitors entered at 12:05.
After the visitors entered at 12:05, the curator unlocked the gallery at noon.
Although the curator unlocked the gallery at noon, the visitors entered at 12:05.
Because the curator unlocked the gallery at noon, the visitors entered at 12:05.
questions.explanation: The introductory clause beginning with after correctly shows that the gallery was unlocked before the visitors entered.
questions.skill: Combining ideas with a subordinating conjunction
questions.topic: Combine Two Sentences - Advanced Grammar Review

questions.prompt: The coach praised the violinist. The violinist had learned the solo. Which sentence correctly combines the ideas with a relative clause?
choices: The coach praised the violinist who had learned the solo.
The coach praised the violinist whom had learned the solo.
The coach praised the violinist which had learned the solo.
The coach praised the violinist whose had learned the solo.
questions.explanation: Who serves as the subject of had learned within the relative clause that identifies the violinist the coach praised.
questions.topic: Activity 3 of 9 (quiz/game): Combine Two Sentences - Advanced Grammar Review

questions.prompt: The museum has one student discount. Visitors must show their IDs. Which sentence correctly combines the ideas with a colon?
choices: The museum has one student discount: visitors must show their IDs.
The museum has one student discount; visitors must show their IDs.
The museum has one student discount, visitors must show their IDs.
The museum has one student discount visitors must show their IDs.
questions.explanation: The colon correctly introduces the specific condition that visitors must show their IDs to receive the student discount.
questions.topic: Activity 3 of 9 (quiz/game): Combine Two Sentences - Advanced Grammar Review

questions.prompt: The museum stays open late on Fridays. Visitors can watch the planetarium show. Which sentence correctly combines the two ideas with a colon?
choices: The museum stays open late on Fridays: visitors can watch the planetarium show.
The museum stays open late on Fridays, visitors can watch the planetarium show.
The museum stays open late on Fridays; visitors can watch the planetarium show.
The museum stays open late on Fridays: and visitors can watch the planetarium show.
questions.explanation: A colon can join two independent clauses when the second clause explains what the first one means.
questions.topic: Combine Two Sentences - Advanced Grammar Review

questions.prompt: The road was icy. That surprised the drivers. Which sentence combines the ideas using a what-clause and a that-clause?
choices: What surprised the drivers was that the road was icy.
What surprised the drivers was the road's icy condition.
What surprised the drivers was that road was icy.
What surprised the drivers was the road was icy.
questions.explanation: The what-clause serves as the subject, and the that-clause identifies the surprising fact that the road was icy.
questions.topic: Combine Two Sentences - Advanced Grammar Review

questions.prompt: The students did not pack snacks. They did not bring water. Which sentence correctly combines the ideas with neither...nor?
choices: The students neither packed snacks nor brought water.
The students neither packed snacks or brought water.
The students not only packed snacks nor brought water.
The students neither packed snacks but nor brought water.
questions.explanation: Neither...nor correctly joins two negative actions and requires nor before the second verb phrase.
questions.topic: Combine Two Sentences - Advanced Grammar Review

questions.prompt: The coach thanked the volunteers. The volunteers had painted the banners. Which sentence combines the ideas using a nonrestrictive relative clause?
choices: The coach thanked the volunteers, who had painted the banners.
The coach thanked the volunteers, whom had painted the banners.
The coach thanked the volunteers, that had painted the banners.
The coach thanked the volunteers, which had painted the banners.
questions.explanation: The clause who had painted the banners adds information about the volunteers and is correctly set off by commas.
questions.topic: Combine Two Sentences - Advanced Grammar Review

questions.prompt: The power failed. The classes moved online. Which sentence places the cause in the introductory clause?
choices: Because the power failed, the classes moved online.
The classes moved online because the power failed.
Although the power failed, the classes moved online.
When the power failed, the classes moved online.
questions.explanation: The introductory dependent clause gives the cause of the classes moving online.
questions.topic: Combine Two Sentences - Advanced Grammar Review

questions.prompt: The first round ended in a draw. The team won the championship in overtime. Which sentence correctly combines the two ideas with a semicolon and a conjunctive adverb?
choices: The first round ended in a draw; however, the team won the championship in overtime.
The first round ended in a draw, however, the team won the championship in overtime.
The first round ended in a draw; however the team won the championship in overtime.
The first round ended in a draw; however, and the team won the championship in overtime.
questions.explanation: A semicolon joins the two independent clauses, and the comma after however separates the conjunctive adverb from the second clause.
questions.skill: Joining independent clauses with a semicolon and a conjunctive adverb
questions.topic: Combine Two Sentences - Advanced Grammar Review

questions.prompt: The photographer adjusted the lens. She wanted the subject to come into focus. Which sentence combines the action and its purpose with in order that?
choices: The photographer adjusted the lens because the subject could come into focus.
The photographer adjusted the lens when the subject could come into focus.
The photographer adjusted the lens in order that the subject could come into focus.
The photographer adjusted the lens although the subject could come into focus.
questions.explanation: In order that introduces a purpose clause explaining that the lens adjustment was intended to bring the subject into focus.
questions.topic: Combine Two Sentences - Advanced Grammar Review

questions.prompt: The library closes at six. Students must return books by then. Which sentence correctly joins the independent clauses with a semicolon?
choices: The library closes at six; students must return books by then.
The library closes at six, students must return books by then.
The library closes at six, and students must return books by then.
The library closes at six; students, must return books by then.
questions.explanation: A semicolon can join two closely related independent clauses without creating a comma splice.
questions.topic: Combine Two Sentences - Advanced Grammar Review

questions.prompt: The trail was muddy. We reached the summit before sunset. Which sentence correctly combines the two ideas with the subordinating conjunction although?
choices: Although the trail was muddy, we reached the summit before sunset.
Although the trail was muddy, and we reached the summit before sunset.
Although the trail was muddy, however we reached the summit before sunset.
Although the trail was muddy, but we reached the summit before sunset.
questions.explanation: Although introduces a dependent clause that contrasts the muddy trail with our arrival before sunset.
questions.skill: Combining sentences with a subordinating conjunction
questions.topic: Combine Two Sentences - Advanced Grammar Review

questions.prompt: The camp offers swimming and kayaking. Students may do both activities. Which sentence correctly combines the ideas with the correlative conjunction both...and?
choices: Students may do both swimming and kayaking at the camp.
Students may do swimming and both kayaking at the camp.
Students may do swimming or both kayaking at the camp.
Both swimming and kayaking may do the students at the camp.
questions.explanation: The correlative conjunction both...and correctly joins the two activities and preserves the meaning that students may participate in each one.
questions.topic: Activity 3 of 9: Combine Two Sentences - Advanced Grammar Review

questions.prompt: The tournament has one rule. Players must wear team jerseys. Which explanation best justifies using a colon to combine these sentences?
choices: The first sentence introduces a specific rule that the second sentence states.
The second sentence gives the reason for the tournament's single rule.
The first sentence gives an example of the rule stated in the second sentence.
The second sentence contrasts the tournament rule with another requirement.
questions.explanation: A colon can introduce the specific rule stated after the broad introductory clause.
questions.topic: Combine Two Sentences - Advanced Grammar Review

questions.prompt: The bakery sells rye bread. The bread is baked each morning. Which sentence correctly joins the two independent clauses with a semicolon?
choices: The bakery sells rye bread; it is baked each morning.
The bakery sells rye bread, it is baked each morning.
The bakery sells rye bread and it is baked each morning.
The bakery sells rye bread, and it is baked each morning.
questions.explanation: The semicolon correctly joins two closely related independent clauses without creating a comma splice.
questions.skill: Joining independent clauses with a semicolon
questions.topic: Combine Two Sentences - Advanced Grammar Review

questions.prompt: Jordan is the team captain. Jordan wears number 12. Which sentence combines the ideas using an appositive?
choices: Jordan, the team captain, wears number 12.
Jordan the team captain, wears number 12.
Jordan, the team captain wears number 12.
Jordan is the team captain, and Jordan wears number 12.
questions.explanation: The team captain is an appositive that renames Jordan and is enclosed by matching commas.
questions.topic: Combine Two Sentences - Advanced Grammar Review

questions.prompt: Which explanation best identifies why the clause because heavy rain flooded the tracks cannot stand alone as a second independent clause after a semicolon?
choices: The clause has a subject and a verb, so a semicolon can join it to the preceding independent clause.
Because is a coordinating conjunction, so it can join two independent clauses with a semicolon.
The clause is a complete sentence, so it should be separated from the first clause by a colon.
The word because makes the clause dependent, so it cannot stand alone as an independent clause joined by a semicolon.
questions.explanation: The word because makes the clause dependent, so it cannot stand alone as an independent clause joined by a semicolon.
questions.topic: Combine Two Sentences - Advanced Grammar Review

questions.prompt: The batteries died. The flashlight stopped working. Which sentence combines the ideas and makes the battery failure the cause?
choices: The flashlight stopped working because the batteries died.
The batteries died because the flashlight stopped working.
The flashlight stopped working although the batteries died.
The flashlight stopped working while the batteries died.
questions.explanation: Because the batteries died introduces a dependent clause that explains why the flashlight stopped working.
questions.skill: Combining clauses to express cause and effect
questions.topic: Activity 3 of 9 (quiz/game): Combine Two Sentences - Advanced Grammar Review

feedback.correct: Nice — you combined the clauses cleanly and earned your serve.

kept.prompt: The rain started. We moved the game indoors. Which sentence uses so to express the cause-and-effect relationship?
choices: The rain started, so we moved the game indoors.
The rain started because we moved the game indoors.
The rain started, although we moved the game indoors.
The rain started, and we moved the game indoors.
kept.explanation: The coordinating conjunction so follows a comma to show that the rain caused the game to be moved indoors.
kept.topic: Combine Two Sentences - Advanced Grammar Review

kept.prompt: The library closes at six. Students must return books by then. Which sentence correctly joins the independent clauses with a semicolon?
choices: The library closes at six; students must return books by then.
The library closes at six, students must return books by then.
The library closes at six, and students must return books by then.
The library closes at six; students, must return books by then.
kept.explanation: A semicolon can join two closely related independent clauses without creating a comma splice.
kept.topic: Combine Two Sentences - Advanced Grammar Review

kept.prompt: The workshop requires three supplies. The supplies are a pen, a notebook, and a pair of scissors. Which sentence correctly introduces the list with a colon?
choices: The workshop requires three supplies: a pen, a notebook, and a pair of scissors.
The workshop requires three supplies, a pen, a notebook, and a pair of scissors.
The workshop requires three supplies; a pen, a notebook, and a pair of scissors.
The workshop requires three supplies because a pen, a notebook, and a pair of scissors.
kept.explanation: The colon appropriately introduces the complete list of supplies after the introductory statement.
kept.skill: Using a colon to introduce a list
kept.topic: Combine Two Sentences - Advanced Grammar Review

kept.prompt: The power failed. The classes moved online. Which sentence places the cause in the introductory clause?
choices: Because the power failed, the classes moved online.
The classes moved online because the power failed.
Although the power failed, the classes moved online.
When the power failed, the classes moved online.
kept.explanation: The introductory dependent clause gives the cause of the classes moving online.
kept.topic: Combine Two Sentences - Advanced Grammar Review

kept.prompt: The bell rang. Everyone left the gym. Which explanation best identifies why the semicolon correctly joins these two independent clauses?
choices: The two independent clauses are closely related, so a semicolon joins them without creating a comma splice.
The second clause is dependent on the first, so a semicolon completes the shared subject and verb.
The two clauses have different subjects, so a semicolon can replace the missing verb in the second clause.
The first clause contains a prepositional phrase, so a semicolon separates it from the main clause.
